title: New becomes normal.
dek: 22 lottery winners rated their happiness 4.00 out of 5, their neighbours 3.82. On Black Friday, why the joy of a new thing is spent in a month and the price is paid for two years.
whyThisIdea: Toate ideile rămase în backlog sunt marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate, așa că am adăugat una nouă, legată de Black Friday de azi: hedonic adaptation (Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman 1978 - câștigătorii la loterie 4.00 vs vecinii 3.82 din 5). Se leagă și de calculul 1.01^365 din recenzia ta la Atomic Habits.

entry.title: New becomes normal.
entry.dek: 22 lottery winners rated their happiness 4.00 out of 5, their neighbours 3.82. On Black Friday, why the joy of a new thing is spent in a month and the price is paid for two years.
body: “The new thing does not stop being good. It stops being new, and I stop noticing the difference.”

Have you ever asked yourself what happened to the thing you wanted so much last year? The phone, the shoes, the headphones you checked the price of every day until you finally bought them. Today is Friday, the 27th of November, it is Black Friday, and a lot of us will buy something today that we have wanted for months. The question is: how long will it still feel like something we wanted? Not how long it will work - how long we will notice it. Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at has a name in psychology, hedonic adaptation, and some people call it the “hedonic treadmill”. The idea is simple: when something in your life gets better (or worse), you feel it strongly at the start, and then you slowly get used to it until it becomes the new normal. I did not meet it in a book. I met it in my own room, looking at things I was very excited about once and now do not even see anymore.

Firstly, let’s split the name in two, the way I like to do. “Hedonic” and “adaptation”. “Hedonic” comes from the Greek word for pleasure, so it is about how good something feels. “Adaptation” is what your eyes do when you walk into a dark room - at first you see nothing, after a few minutes you see everything, and you forget it was ever dark. Put together, it means that <u>the feeling does not stay at the level of the change, it goes back to the level of the normal</u>. The thing is still there. The difference is what disappears.

Secondly, let’s look at the study everybody quotes when they talk about this. In 1978, three psychologists, Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman, published a paper with a very honest title: “Lottery Winners and Accident Victims: Is Happiness Relative?”. They talked to 22 people who had won big in the lottery, to 22 normal people from the same area, and to 29 people who had been paralysed in accidents. Everybody rated how happy they were, on a scale that went up to 5.
Lottery winners: 4.00
People who did not win: 3.82
The difference is 0.18 points, which is 3.6% of the whole scale. A life-changing amount of money, and the people who got it were almost exactly as happy as their neighbours. And there is a second result I find even more interesting: the winners took less pleasure from small everyday things, like hearing a joke or eating breakfast, than the people who never won. The big new thing did not only fade, it made the small old things look smaller.

Now let’s put it a little bit in perspective, with something more normal than a lottery. Let’s say I buy headphones today for €150, and I will use them for 2 years, so 104 weeks. And let’s say the joy of having them halves every week - 100 in the first week, 50 in the second, 25 in the third, and so on. These numbers are my assumptions, not a measurement, but the direction is the one the study points to.
Joy in the first 4 weeks: 100 + 50 + 25 + 12.5 = 187.5 out of about 200, so 93.75%
Money spent in the first 4 weeks: €150 ÷ 104 × 4 = €5.77, so about 4%
So in this model, after one month I have had almost all of the joy and paid almost none of the price. The other 100 weeks cost me €144.23 and give me about 6% of the joy. The price is spread over two years, the excitement is spent in one month.

And this is where it connected with the first book I reviewed here, “Atomic Habits”. The famous calculation is 1.01<sup>365</sup> = 37.78 - get 1% better every day and after a year you are almost 38 times better. But why does nobody feel 38 times better? I think hedonic adaptation is part of the answer. Every day, the new level becomes the normal level, so the 1% is always measured from yesterday, never from the start. The same thing that makes a new phone boring in a month makes your own progress invisible.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. The same study is often told as “people always go back to the same happiness, whatever happens”, and that is not what the numbers say. The people who were paralysed rated their happiness at 2.96, which is 0.86 points below the people who did not win. They adapted to a lot, but not to everything. So adaptation is not a law that erases every change. It is strong with things we get used to seeing every day, and weaker with things that keep hurting, or keep giving, every day. And honestly, for the bad things in life, adaptation is not a problem at all - it is the thing that lets people continue.

So here is what I am going to try, because it is Black Friday and I would rather test this than only write about it. Before I buy anything today, I will ask one question: will I still notice this in week five? Not “will I use it” - I will probably use everything I buy - but will it still feel different from not having it. If the honest answer is no, then I am paying €150 for one good month, and I want to at least know that before I pay.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the idea is right, and it changed how I look at my own wish list. But I have to be honest about two things. First, the halving every week is a number I chose to make the point clear - for some things the joy lasts much longer, and a good pair of shoes I wear every day is not the same as a gadget in a drawer. Second, a study with 22 lottery winners from the 1970s is a small study, nobody measured how happy they were before they won, and I do not want to build my whole life on it. What I take from it is smaller: buying something new is a good first month, not a better life, and it is fine to buy a good first month, as long as I know that is what I am buying.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
